subtopic_detail: Deciding disposition after a first impulsive ingestion when a screening instrument returns a low category
stem:
You are the emergency registrar reviewing a 22 year old apprentice electrician who swallowed fourteen paracetamol tablets in one go six hours ago, twenty minutes after his partner ended their relationship. He told his flatmate within the hour and they drove him in.

His timed paracetamol concentration sits below the treatment line and his liver enzymes and coagulation profile are normal, so the toxicology registrar has cleared him medically and no antidote is required. He says he did it without thinking, is embarrassed, does not want to die now and has no plan. He has never presented before, takes no medication, does not drink or use drugs, and his two flatmates are in the waiting room and have offered to stay with him. The department's structured screening instrument has returned a score in its lowest category, and the consultant asks you to discharge him on that basis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74 beats per minute, blood pressure 122/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Alert and engaged, no psychomotor change, affect reactive, no psychotic features, no self inflicted wounds
data_table.Investigations: Timed paracetamol concentration below the nomogram treatment line, alanine aminotransferase 24 units/L (5-35), international normalised ratio 1.0 (0.8-1.2), electrolytes within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge him with the low risk score documented and advice to see his own doctor
options.rationale: Using a categorical score to authorise discharge is the specific practice that Australian guidance advises against, because these instruments have low positive and negative predictive value at the individual level and most people who go on to die by suicide were categorised as low or moderate risk. Documenting the score gives the appearance of assessment without the content of one. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm

options.text: Admit him to the psychiatric unit because any overdose indicates a high level of risk
options.rationale: Treating every ingestion as requiring admission is the mirror image error and exposes a young man with a first impulsive act, no ongoing intent and present social support to the iatrogenic harms of an admission. Admission is driven by mental state, ongoing intent and the absence of support, none of which apply here. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm

options.text: Repeat the screening instrument in two hours and decide disposition on that score
options.rationale: Repeating an instrument that was never designed to predict individual outcomes does not improve its predictive performance, and the change in score over two hours reflects how settled he feels rather than what he needs. The problem is the use being made of the tool, not the timing of its administration. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm

options.text: Discharge him with a referral letter to a private psychologist and no further follow up
options.rationale: A referral letter transfers responsibility without establishing contact, and uptake of an unassisted referral after self harm is poor, with most patients never attending. The first weeks after an act of self harm are when the repetition risk is concentrated, so the arrangement has to be active rather than nominal. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm

options.text: Complete a collaborative safety plan with means restriction and follow up in a week
options.rationale: Disposition after self harm is decided by a needs based assessment and a plan built with the patient, not by a risk category, and the interventions with actual evidence of benefit are a written safety plan naming warning signs, coping strategies and people to contact, restriction of access to means, and an arranged contact within days. Involving the flatmates in the means restriction turns the available support into something concrete. (Source: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm)
source_refs: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm

explanation.summary: Categorical suicide risk stratification into low, medium and high has been progressively abandoned in Australian practice because its predictive performance at the individual level is close to chance, and because the majority of people who die by suicide were rated below the highest category at their last contact. What replaces it is a needs based formulation that describes the person's current state, the drivers of the act, what has changed since, what supports exist, and what modifiable factors can be acted on now. Safety planning, in which the patient and clinician jointly write down warning signs, internal coping strategies, people and places that provide distraction, contacts for help and steps to make the environment safer, is one of the few interventions with randomised evidence of reduced repetition. Means restriction is the other, and for paracetamol that means limiting quantities kept at home, since impulsive ingestion of what is in the cupboard is the dominant pattern. The period immediately after discharge from an emergency department following self harm carries a markedly elevated risk, which is why arranged contact within days, rather than an unassisted referral, is the standard.
key_points: Categorical risk stratification does not predict individual outcomes and should not set disposition
A needs based formulation and a jointly written safety plan replace it
Means restriction has randomised evidence of benefit and applies to household paracetamol
Arrange an active contact within days rather than sending an unassisted referral
Admission is driven by mental state, ongoing intent and absent support, not by the act itself
explanation.pearls: Paracetamol deserves specific means restriction counselling in Australia because ingestion is usually impulsive and uses whatever is in the house: reducing the quantity stored at home is the single most effective environmental intervention, and the same conversation should cover securing any firearms and limiting stored medication for everyone in the household.

sources.label: Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Psychiatrists: Clinical practice guideline for the management of deliberate self-harm
Australian Institute of Health and Welfare: Suicide and self-harm monitoring

subtopic_detail: Burning upper abdominal discomfort partly controlled by six weeks of self prescribed acid suppression at forty two
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 42 year old truck dispatcher with three months of burning discomfort high in the abdomen, worse after meals and sometimes waking him at night. Six weeks ago he bought esomeprazole from the pharmacy and has taken it every morning since.

He says he is about sixty per cent better on it but that the burning returns within two days whenever he forgets. He has no difficulty or pain on swallowing, has not vomited, has lost no weight, and has seen no blood or black material in his stool. He takes no anti-inflammatory drugs, drinks four standard drinks a week and has never smoked. His parents were born in Vietnam and no relative has had stomach cancer.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg/m2, mild epigastric tenderness without guarding, no mass, no hepatosplenomegaly, no supraclavicular lymphadenopathy, conjunctivae not pale
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-175), mean cell volume 89 fL (80-100), ferritin 96 micrograms/L (30-300), liver function and lipase within normal limits, faecal occult blood negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for gastroscopy while he continues the proton pump inhibitor
options.rationale: Endoscopy is indicated for dyspepsia with alarm features such as dysphagia, vomiting, weight loss, bleeding or anaemia, or for new dyspepsia over about fifty five, and he has none of these at forty two. Acid suppression also heals and masks lesions, so scoping on treatment lowers the yield further. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Stop the proton pump inhibitor for two weeks then arrange a urea breath test
options.rationale: Uninvestigated dyspepsia without alarm features in a patient under fifty five is managed by testing for Helicobacter pylori and eradicating it if present, and his family origin places him in a group with substantially higher prevalence. Acid suppression suppresses bacterial urease activity and produces false negative breath and stool tests, so the drug is withheld for two weeks before testing, as antibiotics and bismuth are for four. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Arrange a urea breath test now while he continues his current treatment
options.rationale: The test is the right one but performing it on treatment is the classic error, because suppressed urease activity and reduced bacterial load give a false negative in a substantial minority. A negative result obtained this way would wrongly close off the diagnosis. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Double the proton pump inhibitor dose and review his symptoms in eight weeks
options.rationale: Escalating acid suppression may improve symptoms further but leaves an eradicable infection untreated, with its associated risks of peptic ulceration and, over decades, gastric malignancy. Long term acid suppression without a diagnosis is also how patients end up on these drugs indefinitely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal)

options.text: Arrange serology for Helicobacter pylori and treat him if the result is positive
options.rationale: Antibody testing cannot distinguish current infection from one cleared years ago, because antibodies persist long after eradication, so a positive result in a population with high background prevalence would lead to treating many people who are not infected. It is not recommended for diagnosis in Australia. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: Uninvestigated dyspepsia in a patient under about fifty five with no alarm features is managed by a test and treat strategy for Helicobacter pylori rather than by endoscopy, which reduces both cost and the number of normal procedures without missing significant disease. Alarm features that override this and mandate endoscopy are dysphagia, odynophagia, persistent vomiting, unintentional weight loss, gastrointestinal bleeding or iron deficiency anaemia, an epigastric mass, and a family history of upper gastrointestinal malignancy. Prevalence of the organism in Australia is around fifteen per cent in the general population but considerably higher in people born in, or whose families come from, East and Southeast Asia, Eastern Europe, the Middle East and South America, and in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. Diagnosis uses the urea breath test or stool antigen, both of which require acid suppression to be stopped two weeks beforehand and antibiotics or bismuth four weeks beforehand, while serology is not recommended because it cannot separate current from past infection. Eradication uses a seven day course of a proton pump inhibitor with amoxicillin and clarithromycin, and confirmation of cure by breath test at least four weeks after finishing is recommended.
key_points: Test and treat for the organism rather than endoscopy in patients under fifty five without alarm features
Alarm features are dysphagia, vomiting, weight loss, bleeding, anaemia or an epigastric mass
Acid suppression must be stopped two weeks before breath or stool testing
Serology cannot distinguish current from past infection and is not recommended
Confirm eradication with a breath test at least four weeks after treatment
explanation.pearls: Confirmation of cure is not optional in Australian practice because clarithromycin resistance now runs at well over ten per cent in much of the country, so a repeat urea breath test at least four weeks after the course, again off acid suppression for two weeks, is arranged at the time the prescription is written rather than left to chance.

subtopic_detail: Negative coeliac serology in a woman who began a strict gluten free diet two months before the blood test
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 32 year old woman who has had twelve months of bloating, loose stools and fatigue. Two months ago, after reading about it online, she cut out all gluten and says her bowels settled within a fortnight and her energy improved.

The locum ordered tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A antibodies before her last appointment and the result is negative, with a normal total immunoglobulin A. She has a younger sister with type 1 diabetes. She and her partner are planning a pregnancy next year and she wants to know whether she actually has to avoid gluten for life or whether she can stop bothering.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 21 kg/m2, pale conjunctivae, no mouth ulcers, no rash over the elbows or knees, abdomen soft and non-tender
data_table.Investigations: Tissue transglutaminase immunoglobulin A antibodies negative with normal total immunoglobulin A, haemoglobin 108 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 76 fL (80-100), ferritin 9 micrograms/L (30-300), thyroid stimulating hormone 2.0 mIU/L (0.4-4.0)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Accept the negative result and manage her as having irritable bowel syndrome
options.rationale: The serology cannot be interpreted because the antibodies fall and often disappear within weeks of gluten withdrawal, so this is an uninterpretable test rather than a negative one. Iron deficiency anaemia and a first degree relative with an autoimmune condition also make a functional label premature. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

options.text: Arrange duodenal biopsy now while she continues her gluten free diet
options.rationale: Villous architecture recovers on a gluten free diet in the same way the serology normalises, so biopsy taken after two months of exclusion can be entirely normal in established disease. Biopsy is the right test, but only after gluten has been reintroduced. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Arrange faecal calprotectin and refer for colonoscopy if it is raised
options.rationale: Faecal calprotectin discriminates inflammatory bowel disease from functional symptoms and colonoscopy examines the wrong part of the bowel for this question, since the disease being considered affects the proximal small intestine. Neither addresses the diagnostic problem created by the diet. (Source: Gastroenterological Society of Australia)

options.text: Advise a gluten challenge for six weeks and then repeat the serology
options.rationale: Both the antibody test and the duodenal histology depend on ongoing gluten exposure, so an adequate challenge, conventionally four slices of wheat bread or equivalent each day for six weeks, must precede retesting. Establishing the diagnosis properly matters more than usual here because of the lifelong diet, the family screening implications and the pregnancy she is planning. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

options.text: Arrange coeliac associated genetic typing and stop testing if it is positive
options.rationale: Genetic typing is useful in exactly the opposite direction: around half the Australian population carries one of the permissive alleles so a positive result excludes nothing, while a negative result makes the disease virtually impossible and can spare a challenge. Its value is in ruling out, not ruling in. (Source: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease)
source_refs: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease

explanation.summary: The commonest reason for an uninterpretable coeliac result in general practice is that the patient has already removed gluten, because both the serology and the duodenal histology normalise on a gluten free diet, often within weeks to months. The diagnosis matters even when symptoms have settled on the diet, because a formal diagnosis brings first degree relative screening, bone density assessment, nutritional monitoring, and access to support and to subsidised food products, and because the lifelong strictness required differs from that of self managed gluten avoidance. Untreated disease in a woman planning pregnancy is associated with iron and folate deficiency, low birth weight and recurrent miscarriage, which sharpens the case for resolving the question now. The standard sequence is serology first, then referral for duodenal biopsy while still consuming gluten, with genetic typing reserved for cases where a challenge is impossible or where a negative result would end the question. Iron deficiency anaemia with a low mean cell volume in a menstruating woman with bowel symptoms is a classic presentation and should never be treated with iron alone without asking why.
key_points: Serology and histology both normalise on a gluten free diet, making tests uninterpretable
An adequate challenge is about four slices of wheat bread daily for six weeks
A formal diagnosis triggers relative screening, bone density and nutritional follow up
Genetic typing has value for excluding the disease, not for confirming it
Untreated disease in pregnancy is linked to low birth weight and miscarriage
explanation.pearls: Warn her before she starts that a challenge after two months off gluten is often far more symptomatic than her original illness, and that the alternative if she cannot complete six weeks is to test the permissive genetic alleles, since a negative result there effectively excludes the disease and ends the need for the diet.

sources.label: Coeliac Australia: Diagnosis of coeliac disease
Royal Australian College of General Practitioners

subtopic_detail: Progressive oedema with 6 g of daily proteinuria and albumin 24 g/L in a previously well man of forty
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 40 year old warehouse supervisor referred with three weeks of leg swelling that now reaches his thighs, and puffiness around his eyes that is worst when he wakes. He mentions that the toilet bowl is full of froth in the mornings.

He has never been unwell, takes no regular medication and no anti-inflammatory drugs, and has no rash, joint pain or recent infection. Urine microscopy shows no red cells, no red cell casts and no dysmorphic cells. His blood pressure is 142/88 mmHg on repeated measurement.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 142/88 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Pitting oedema to the mid thigh bilaterally, periorbital puffiness, no rash, no lymphadenopathy, jugular venous pressure not elevated, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Urine protein to creatinine ratio 620 mg/mmol (less than 30), serum albumin 24 g/L (35-50), creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), total cholesterol 8.4 mmol/L, hepatitis B and C and human immunodeficiency virus serology negative, antinuclear antibody negative, fasting glucose within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for renal biopsy and start an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor
options.rationale: Heavy proteinuria with hypoalbuminaemia, oedema and hyperlipidaemia, in an adult with a bland urinary sediment and negative secondary screen, requires tissue to identify which glomerular lesion is present, because the histology dictates whether immunosuppression is used and which agent. Blockade of the renin angiotensin system is started in parallel because it reduces proteinuria and controls the blood pressure whatever the biopsy shows. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

options.text: Start high dose prednisolone and review his proteinuria in four weeks
options.rationale: Empirical corticosteroid without histology is standard practice in children, in whom minimal change disease accounts for the great majority of cases, but in adults the range of lesions is wide and several of them respond poorly or not at all to steroids. Treating blind risks months of steroid exposure for a lesion that needed something else. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

options.text: Start a loop diuretic alone and review his proteinuria in four weeks
options.rationale: Diuresis with salt restriction is a necessary part of symptom control and will be used alongside the correct answer, but as the sole plan it treats the oedema while the glomerular lesion continues unchecked towards chronic kidney disease. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

options.text: Start prophylactic anticoagulation and review his proteinuria in four weeks
options.rationale: Thrombosis is a genuine hazard of this syndrome, and prophylactic anticoagulation is considered once the histology is known, particularly for membranous nephropathy with an albumin below 20 to 25 g/L. It is an adjunct decided after the biopsy rather than the step that replaces it. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of chest abdomen and pelvis to seek a malignancy
options.rationale: An occult solid organ malignancy is a recognised secondary cause of membranous nephropathy and is worth pursuing in older patients, but age appropriate screening rather than whole body imaging is the accepted approach, and it follows rather than precedes the histological diagnosis. (Source: Kidney Health Australia)

explanation.summary: Nephrotic syndrome is defined by proteinuria above 3.5 g per day, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema, usually with hyperlipidaemia, and the urine protein to creatinine ratio in milligrams per millimole approximates the daily protein loss in milligrams per day divided by ten, so a ratio of 620 corresponds to about 6 g. A bland sediment with no red cells or casts points to a purely nephrotic lesion rather than a nephritic one, and in Australian adults the commonest underlying diagnoses are membranous nephropathy, focal segmental glomerulosclerosis and minimal change disease. Adults need a biopsy because these lesions cannot be told apart clinically and their treatments differ, whereas children under ten with typical features are treated empirically with corticosteroid. Complications to anticipate are venous and arterial thrombosis from urinary loss of antithrombin, infection from loss of immunoglobulin, acute kidney injury from intravascular depletion, and accelerated atherosclerosis. Supportive management is common to all causes: salt restriction, loop diuretic, blockade of the renin angiotensin system, statin therapy and vaccination.
key_points: A protein to creatinine ratio of 620 mg/mmol corresponds to roughly 6 g of daily loss
A bland urinary sediment distinguishes a nephrotic from a nephritic lesion
Adults require biopsy because the treatable lesions cannot be separated clinically
Children with typical features are treated empirically with corticosteroid instead
Blockade of the renin angiotensin system reduces proteinuria whatever the histology
explanation.pearls: Suspect renal vein thrombosis if he develops sudden flank pain, visible haematuria or an unexplained rise in creatinine, because urinary loss of antithrombin makes this syndrome genuinely prothrombotic, and the risk is highest in membranous nephropathy with a serum albumin below 20 g/L.

subtopic_detail: Preparing a patient on three antihypertensives for an aldosterone to renin ratio with potassium 3.2
stem:
You are the general medicine registrar seeing a 46 year old teacher whose blood pressure remains 168/102 mmHg despite perindopril 10 mg, amlodipine 10 mg and hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. Her pharmacy dispensing record and her home readings both confirm she is taking them.

She takes no potassium supplement, no liquorice and no anti-inflammatory drugs. She does not snore and has no daytime sleepiness, and there is no abdominal bruit. Her renal function is normal and her renal ultrasound showed two normal sized kidneys. You decide to screen her for an excess of mineralocorticoid.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 76 beats per minute, blood pressure 168/102 mmHg, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, SpO2 98 percent on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 27 kg/m2, no Cushingoid features, no abdominal bruit, no radiofemoral delay, fundi with arteriovenous nipping only
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 143 mmol/L (135-145), bicarbonate 30 mmol/L (22-32), creatinine 72 micromol/L (45-90), urine albumin to creatinine ratio 4.2 mg/mmol (less than 3.5)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate preparation before the blood test?

options.text: Stop the amlodipine for four weeks and replace it with spironolactone cover
options.rationale: This inverts the rule. Mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists are the single class that most reliably invalidates the test by raising renin, and they must be withheld for at least four to six weeks; the calcium channel blocker has only a minor effect and can usually be continued. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Stop all three of her agents for four weeks with no antihypertensive cover
options.rationale: Leaving a blood pressure of 168/102 mmHg untreated for a month to purify a screening test exposes her to stroke and cardiac events for no diagnostic gain, since agents that do not disturb the ratio are available as cover. Complete withdrawal is not required. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Correct the potassium, stop the thiazide for four weeks and use prazosin cover
options.rationale: Hypokalaemia directly suppresses aldosterone secretion and can produce a falsely normal ratio, so the potassium is corrected before testing, and potassium wasting diuretics are withheld for four weeks because they raise renin. An alpha blocker, slow release verapamil or hydralazine provides blood pressure cover without disturbing the measurement. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Proceed with the test now because none of her current drugs affect the ratio
options.rationale: Her thiazide and her hypokalaemia both push the result towards a false negative, so a normal ratio obtained under these conditions would not exclude the diagnosis and would end the workup prematurely. A positive result under these conditions, by contrast, would still be meaningful. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

options.text: Stop the perindopril for four weeks and continue her other two drugs unchanged
options.rationale: Blockade of the renin angiotensin system raises renin and therefore lowers the ratio, so it also biases towards a false negative, but it is generally regarded as acceptable to continue because the direction of the error is conservative. Stopping it while leaving the thiazide and the hypokalaemia in place corrects the smaller problem and leaves the larger ones. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia)

explanation.summary: Primary aldosteronism is the commonest specifically treatable cause of hypertension, present in roughly five to ten per cent of all hypertensive patients and closer to twenty per cent of those with resistant hypertension, and it carries excess cardiovascular and renal risk beyond that explained by the blood pressure alone. Only a minority are hypokalaemic, so a normal potassium does not exclude it and screening is indicated in resistant hypertension, hypertension with spontaneous or diuretic induced hypokalaemia, an adrenal incidentaloma, or hypertension with a family history of early stroke. Screening is by the plasma aldosterone to renin ratio drawn mid morning after the patient has been up for at least two hours and seated for five to fifteen minutes. Interpretation depends entirely on preparation: hypokalaemia must be corrected, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists withheld for four to six weeks and potassium wasting diuretics for four weeks, while alpha blockers, slow release verapamil and hydralazine are the safe cover agents. A positive ratio is followed by a confirmatory suppression test and then adrenal vein sampling to separate a unilateral adenoma, which is cured by laparoscopic adrenalectomy, from bilateral hyperplasia, which is treated medically.
key_points: Only a minority of cases are hypokalaemic, so normal potassium does not exclude it
Hypokalaemia suppresses aldosterone and must be corrected before testing
Mineralocorticoid antagonists are withheld four to six weeks and thiazides four weeks
Alpha blockers, slow release verapamil and hydralazine are the safe cover agents
A positive ratio is followed by a confirmatory test and then adrenal vein sampling
explanation.pearls: Remember the direction of each interference rather than a list: drugs that raise renin, including diuretics and blockade of the renin angiotensin system, push the ratio down and cause false negatives, so a positive result on those drugs is still trustworthy, whereas beta blockers lower renin and cause false positives that must be confirmed.
